difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: one concept (logical equivalence of propositional formulas) settled by recalling p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q or a 4-row truth table, about 1 min for a prepared student.
stem:
Let $p$ and $q$ be any two propositions. Consider the following propositional statements.

$$S_1 : p ightarrow q, \quad S_2 : 
eg p \land q, \quad S_3 : 
eg p \lor q, \quad S_4 : 
eg p \lor 
eg q,$$

where $\land$ denotes conjunction (AND operation), $\lor$ denotes disjunction (OR operation), and $
eg$ denotes negation (NOT operation). Which one of the following options is correct? (Note: $\equiv$ denotes logical equivalence)

solution.quick: The implication $p \rightarrow q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. $\neg p \lor q$ is also false exactly in that one case. So $S_1 \equiv S_3$ (the implication law). Every other pair differs on at least one row of the truth table. Answer **(A)**.

steps.title: What logical equivalence means
steps.body: Two formulas are logically equivalent ($\equiv$) when they have the **same truth value for every assignment** of truth values to $p$ and $q$. With two variables there are only $2^2 = 4$ assignments, so a truth table settles each option. One row where the columns differ is enough to show that two formulas are *not* equivalent.

steps.title: Build the truth table
steps.body:
Recall that $p \rightarrow q$ is false **only** when $p = \text{T}$ and $q = \text{F}$.

| $p$ | $q$ | $S_1: p \rightarrow q$ | $S_2: \neg p \land q$ | $S_3: \neg p \lor q$ | $S_4: \neg p \lor \neg q$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T | T | T | F | T | F |
| T | F | F | F | F | T |
| F | T | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | T | F | T | T |

steps.title: Compare the columns for each option
steps.body:
- **(A) $S_1$ vs $S_3$:** $(\text{T},\text{F},\text{T},\text{T})$ and $(\text{T},\text{F},\text{T},\text{T})$ agree in all four rows, so they are **equivalent**.
- **(B) $S_2$ vs $S_3$:** these differ at $(p,q) = (\text{T},\text{T})$, where $S_2 = \text{F}$ and $S_3 = \text{T}$, and also at $(\text{F},\text{F})$, so they are not equivalent.
- **(C) $S_2$ vs $S_4$:** these differ at $(p,q) = (\text{T},\text{F})$, where $S_2 = \text{F}$ and $S_4 = \text{T}$, and also at $(\text{F},\text{F})$, so they are not equivalent.
- **(D) $S_1$ vs $S_4$:** these differ at $(p,q) = (\text{T},\text{T})$, where $S_1 = \text{T}$ and $S_4 = \text{F}$, and also at $(\text{T},\text{F})$, so they are not equivalent.

steps.title: Confirm algebraically
steps.body:
- Implication elimination: $p ightarrow q \equiv 
eg p \lor q$, so $S_1 \equiv S_3$ directly.
- De Morgan: $S_4 = 
eg p \lor 
eg q \equiv 
eg(p \land q)$ (NAND). It is false only when both $p$ and $q$ are true.
- $S_2 = 
eg p \land q \equiv 
eg(p \lor 
eg q) \equiv 
eg(q ightarrow p)$. It is true in exactly one row ($p = 	ext{F}, q = 	ext{T}$), so it cannot match any of the other three, which are each true in three rows.

Only option **(A)** is correct.

solution.teaching:
**Propositions and connectives.** A proposition is a statement that is either true (T) or false (F). Connectives build new statements from old ones. $\neg p$ flips the value. $p \land q$ is true only when both are true. $p \lor q$ is true when at least one is true.

**Material implication.** $p \rightarrow q$ ("if $p$ then $q$") makes a promise: whenever $p$ holds, $q$ holds. The promise is broken only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. When $p$ is false, the promise is not tested, so the implication counts as true ("vacuously true"). This is exactly the behaviour of $\neg p \lor q$: it is false only when $\neg p$ is false (so $p$ is true) **and** $q$ is false. That is why the identity

$$p \rightarrow q \;\equiv\; \neg p \lor q$$

is one of the most-used rewrites in logic. It is how implications are turned into clauses for resolution and CNF conversion.

**Logical equivalence.** $A \equiv B$ means that $A \leftrightarrow B$ is a tautology, i.e. the two truth-table columns are identical. To *prove* an equivalence you check all rows or use known laws (De Morgan, distribution, implication elimination). To *disprove* one, a single counterexample row is enough.

**Useful companions.** De Morgan's laws, $\neg(p \land q) \equiv \neg p \lor \neg q$ and $\neg(p \lor q) \equiv \neg p \land \neg q$. The contrapositive, $p \rightarrow q \equiv \neg q \rightarrow \neg p$. The converse $q \rightarrow p$ is **not** equivalent to $p \rightarrow q$.

**Back to the question.** $S_1$ is an implication and $S_3$ is its disjunctive form, so they are equivalent and (A) is correct. $S_2$ (true in one row) and $S_4$ (false in one row) are different functions from each other and from $S_1$. A single row refutes each of (B), (C) and (D).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Implication elimination: $p \rightarrow q \equiv \neg p \lor q$. Both columns are $(\text{T},\text{F},\text{T},\text{T})$, false only when $p = \text{T}, q = \text{F}$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\neg p \land q$ and $\neg p \lor q$ differ only in the connective, but at $p = q = \text{T}$ the first is F and the second is T (they also differ at $p = q = \text{F}$).

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation:
$
eg p \land q$ is true only at $(	ext{F},	ext{T})$, while $
eg p \lor 
eg q \equiv 
eg(p \land q)$ is true in three rows. For example, at $(	ext{F},	ext{F})$ they give F and T.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation:
$S_1 \equiv 
eg p \lor q$, whereas $S_4 = 
eg p \lor 
eg q$ has $
eg q$ in place of $q$. At $p = q = 	ext{T}$, $S_1 = 	ext{T}$ but $S_4 = 	ext{F}$, and at $(	ext{T},	ext{F})$, $S_1 = 	ext{F}$ but $S_4 = 	ext{T}$.

solution.shortcut: Memorise $p \rightarrow q \equiv \neg p \lor q$, which gives (A) immediately. To double-check the rest, the single row $p = q = \text{F}$ gives $S_2 = \text{F}$ but $S_3 = S_4 = \text{T}$, ruling out (B) and (C). The row $p = q = \text{T}$ gives $S_1 = \text{T}$ but $S_4 = \text{F}$, ruling out (D).
solution.commonTrap:
Misremembering the implication law. The correct rewrite negates **only the antecedent** and keeps OR: $p ightarrow q \equiv 
eg p \lor q$. Negating both parts gives $
eg p \lor 
eg q$, which is really $p ightarrow 
eg q$, and leads to (D). Replacing OR by AND gives $
eg p \land q$, which is really $
eg(q ightarrow p)$. That makes $S_1$ look like $S_2$ instead of $S_3$, so (A) looks wrong. A related slip is forgetting that an implication with a false antecedent is (vacuously) true, i.e. reading $p ightarrow q$ as $p \land q$ (column T, F, F, F) or as $p \leftrightarrow q$ (column T, F, F, T). Then no column in the table matches $S_1$ and the correct option (A) looks wrong. Finally, $S_2 = 
eg p \land q$ and $S_3 = 
eg p \lor q$ differ by one symbol, so misreading one as the other makes (B) look correct.

transcription.notes: Transcribed from the official paper rendering and independently checked against it. The four statements S1-S4, which the paper prints on one line, are set as a single display-math line in the same order and with the same connectives (S1: p -> q, S2: not p AND q, S3: not p OR q, S4: not p OR not q). The definitions of AND, OR and NOT, the equivalence note, and options (A)-(D) match the paper verbatim.

answerVerification.notes: Blind re-solve (done before reading the stored solution): p -> q is false only at (p,q) = (T,F), and so is ~p v q, so S1 is equivalent to S3 and option (A) is correct. This agrees with the official key A. The Python truth table over the rows (T,T),(T,F),(F,T),(F,F) gives S1 = S3 = (T,F,T,T), S2 = (F,F,T,F), S4 = (F,T,T,T). Option B fails at (T,T) and (F,F), C at (T,F) and (F,F), and D at (T,T) and (T,F). Exactly one option (A) holds.
